title: Giving first
hookLine: in the gradual talk the Buddha taught giving before anything else

cards: If you were going to explain Buddhism to someone who had never heard of it, where would you start? The usual guesses: the four noble truths. Meditation.

Suffering, emptiness, the lotus position. The early texts describe how the Buddha himself often started with people who came to him fresh, and it wasn't any of those. He started with something a child can do.
Something you could do before you finish this sentence.

teach.h: THE GRADUAL TALK: A TALK IN STEPS.
teach.b: It's called the gradual talk, anupubbikatha, a talk in steps.

The texts describe it again and again when the Buddha meets a newcomer, like Yasa, a rich young man who ran out of his house one night unable to stand his own life. The Buddha begins with dana, giving.
Then sila, virtue, which you've just spent a week on.

Then the heavens, the happy results of good actions, then the drawbacks of chasing pleasure, then the relief of letting go. Only when the listener's mind is ready, soft, open and glad, does he teach the four noble truths.

teach.h: A CLEAN CLOTH TAKES THE DYE.
teach.b: The texts compare it to a clean cloth taking dye evenly. Why does giving come first? Because it's the easiest place to feel what the whole path is about.
When you give, you open your hand, and for a moment the grip of mine loosens. That loosening is a small taste of the freedom the rest of the teaching points to.
Giving is also one of the perfections, the qualities a bodhisattva, a Buddha-to-be, develops over many lives. You met Vessantara, the prince who gave everything, back in the stories camp.
But the gradual talk doesn't start with a prince giving away a kingdom. It starts with food, a coin, a cup of water.
Giving opens the door; everything else walks through it.

how: Buddhist teachers often begin with generosity, as the Buddha did in the gradual talk; many Buddhists give food to monks, support their temple and give to those in need as the everyday ground of practice.

o: the Buddha began his teaching with giving
you must give before you can meditate
the Buddha's first sermon was on charity

games.q: match the step of the gradual talk.
p: taught when the mind is ready

s: with a lay newcomer like Yasa, the Buddha opened with the four noble truths
in the gradual talk he began with giving, then virtue, and taught the truths last.
in the gradual talk, virtue comes before giving
giving comes first, then virtue, then the rest.
giving is listed among the perfections a bodhisattva develops
Vessantara's story, from the stories camp, is about that perfection.

games.q: you're the Buddha. Yasa, a rich young man sick of his own life, sits down in front of you, knowing nothing of your teaching. what do you talk about first?
games.why: the texts say he began the gradual talk with giving, then virtue, and taught the four truths only when Yasa's mind was ready.

practice: Make a fist with one hand, not tight, just closed, and notice what it feels like to hold on. Then slowly open it, palm up on your knee, and breathe with the open hand, feeling the air on your palm.
If you like, think of one small thing you could give: a coffee, a coin, a compliment, your place in line.

wordCard.voice: Giving first. In the gradual talk, the Buddha began with dana, giving, before virtue and before the four noble truths.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: giving, generosity; the first step of the gradual talk.

carryVoice: Your line: giving opens the door. In the gradual talk, giving comes before everything else. That's day one hundred thirty-one.
